blocks.text: Since time immemorial, a temple—whether open or closed—has been the central gathering place for human communities, a place for sharing creation, spirituality, exchange, and respect. Very often, by its very design, it symbolizes elevation, inquiry, and individual physical—or even metaphysical—sacrifice. However, for several millennia now, there is evidence that many of these places—dedicated to the pursuit of absolute beauty—have been plundered by a kind of vulgar greed. The list is endless: from the Golden Calf to the plundering of Egypt, from Delphi to Jayavarman VIII, from Philip IV “the Fair” to the merchants of the Temple, and so on. Whether in terms of their (material) contents or their (philosophical) symbolism, many temples have, despite themselves, become sources of profit. It is interesting to note in passing that modern tourism supports the profit-making schemes of these plunderers; whether these sites lie dormant (more or less dilapidated) or are still functioning as originally intended, visitors are asked to pay to access them—and rarely does this benefit the disciples and the custodians. There are even cases where the custodians and users of these sites are asked to vacate—at least temporarily—to ensure the profiteers’ commercial commitments. The height of irony, isn’t it?
Why should the temple of photography be exempt from this observation of disheartening situations?

We have all observed in recent years—broadly speaking, since the beginning of this new century—that our world is sinking relentlessly into the same decline as all other realms, whether material or spiritual, past or present.

Our calling, our ideal, and our commitment to all that stems from the marvelous techniques of photography are being eroded in the quagmire of immediate financial gain, unreasonable speculation, and suffocating parasitism. I would like to qualify this—very real—verdict by pointing out that this disastrous outcome was forged with the active (albeit naïve) complicity of a great many of us. The siren song and the “better days” always end in irreversible calamities.
This is how, every day, we discover a new flint that carves out our grave by robing of our common good: creativity, spirituality, exchange, and respect.
The list is long of all those little trifles that lead to a debacle.

Photographs (30 cm x 40 cm) sold for 5 euros at a photography festival that claims to be international in scope. This can’t be true! How—even if these photographs were of no interest—can the artist and the organizers be complicit in such a travesty for the entire community? This isn’t even just a meager profit anymore; it’s a massacre! Shame on all these organizers who, just to earn enough to pay for a display stand and five meters of hanging space, are tearing down a legacy.

Proposals from a major American publisher (and the Europeans, not to be outdone, have easely followed suit) who scours exhibitions to contact targeted exhibitors and offer them the opportunity to produce—or rather, cobble together—a book featuring their works. The production of the book will cost the unsuspecting artist—desperate for recognition—$24,000. The icing on the cake is that the publisher excludes the book from its distribution networks. Here you go, my good friend—you can walk away with your 1,000 copies under your arm. Not everyone has 1,000 friends to give them to.

In real estate, we call these people “con artists.” It’s the kind of thing where “my gallery” or “my international organization” offers to host an exhibition of your—so-called—wonderful works. The bait is set—you need to look closely before taking the bait with the hook. The list of conditions—both stated and unstated—is generally as impressive as it is devastating to your bank account. Your so-called promoter is really just a money-squeezer who tracks potential sources of profit in his well-honed role as a leech.

From real estate to stagnation, the arrival of government agencies—in all their forms—in our field, which they completely ignore (with rare exceptions), is increasingly aimed at imposing their operating rules on us and advancing their career plans rather than at enriching us. Although, at times, some of their members are not entirely indifferent to the crumbs from our events. The inherent inertia of these large structures—whether public or private—gives the impression of coming to the rescue of a victory, but in reality, it shuts down any debate on potential future developments. We often have to count ourselves lucky when their rhetoric doesn’t stifle or distort the few initiatives that remain.

We are also all aware of the various attempts to “uberize” our expertise and creativity while simultaneously devouring the entirety of our work. The “take pictures for me and, above all, don’t worry about a thing” mentality. To this day, the individualism and independence of true photographers have consistently rejected the terms of this “brave new world.” The question remains: how long can the financial livelihood of photographic artists withstand these steamrollers that are taking hold in the global economic landscape?

The latest scheme concocted by all these gold diggers, born out of our photographs, is the art subscription. It’s no longer just the photographer who’s being fleeced; the amateur collector is now also among the sheep to be sheared. There’s no such thing as a small profit—the more of us who pay, the juicier the haul. It’s all very simple: you pay a monthly subscription fee—no, it’s even simpler than that: a monthly subscription fee is automatically deducted from your account (and is very difficult to cancel). In return, you receive some random photographic image on high-quality paper (reproductions, copies made from originals, offset prints, etc.) that has been specially selected for you. An uninteresting photograph that’s exorbitantly priced for what it is, which you must hasten to store under strict archival conditions as soon as you receive it. Such an artistic masterpiece demands nothing less. The big unknown remains the uncertain compensation for the artist who was imprudent enough to let their file slip into the web.

This is how all these middlemen—who, more often than not, know nothing about the photographic image, whether in terms of its technical execution or its historical or creative expression—line their pockets handsomely. All they have to do is walk through the doors of our temple, if they aren’t already shamelessly setting themselves up there. Many photographers have been duped by all these snake-oil salesmen who promised them the moon and the stars. Today, it is all these creative forces that are struggling to survive in the midst of a real economic crisis. Following the principle of communicating vessels, the income generated by their talent has flowed from their pockets into the virtual coffers of all these numerous parasites.

What is becoming increasingly difficult to accept is the realization that today’s sheep no longer have wool on their backs—due to negligence and a lack of solidarity in the face of danger. The total lack of preparation evident among our successors is unlikely to improve this alarming situation.
